text: Hanoi hosts an international stage for local and global craft villages
Held in the lead-up to Vietnam Culture Day on November 24, the first Global Craft Village Conservation and Development Festival 2026 was both a celebration and a commitment.

It honored the master artisans and skilled workers who have kept Vietnam's crafts alive for centuries, and showed that, with the support of every level of government and the partnership of the international community, Vietnamese craft villages are ready to stand among the world's great centers of craftsmanship.

The capital welcomed the World Craft Council and artisans from nearly 60 countries and territories as well as World Craft Council Representatives - a clear sign that Vietnam's centuries-old craft villages are ready to take their place in the global creative economy.
For six days, the world's craft community turned its eyes toward Hanoi.

The first Global Craft Village Conservation and Development Festival 2026, with the theme "Converging Craft Village Identity - Connecting Global Excellence," opened on the evening of November 13 at the Thang Long Imperial Citadel, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, with its main program running until November 16 and other side events taking place from November 12-17.

Organized by the Hanoi People's Committee in coordination with the Ministry of Agriculture and Environment under Joint Plan No. 395/KHLT-UBND-BNNMT, the Festival is the first event of its kind and scale in Vietnam.
It brought together leaders from the World Craft Council (WCC), ambassadors, international organizations, and around 200 artisans and designers.
Its message is simple: Vietnam's craft villages are no longer only a heritage to be protected, but a creative force that the State is actively helping to reach the world.
Few places in the world hold as much living craft heritage as Hanoi.

The capital counts around 1,350 villages practicing crafts, of which 337 are officially recognized as craft villages and traditional craft villages, preserving 47 of Vietnam's national traditional crafts.
Hanoi's handicrafts already reach markets in 89 countries and territories.
That heritage is now earning international recognition.

Four Hanoi villages - Bat Trang ceramics, Van Phuc silk, Son Dong sculpture and lacquer, and Chuyen My mother-of-pearl inlay - are members of the WCC's World Craft Cities network, with Son Dong and Chuyen My admitted earlier this year.
Vietnam now ranks second in the world by number of members in the network, and Hanoi has set itself the goal of nominating further villages.

The Festival journey began on November 12 at the Hanoi Department of Agriculture and Environment, where Department leaders received WCC delegations together with representatives of Bat Trang, Ha Dong, Son Dong, and Chuyen My.

The working session reviewed what the four villages have achieved since joining the network, prepared for the Council's upcoming periodic assessments, and discussed the content of an MoU to place cooperation between Hanoi and the WCC on a long-term footing.
On November 13, the Ministry of Agriculture and Environment and the Hanoi People's Committee formally welcomed the international delegations.
The exchange of greetings and gifts between Vietnamese leaders and guests from across the world reflected the spirit of the Festival: craft as a language of friendship between nations.
That evening, beneath the Doan Mon Gate of the Thang Long Imperial Citadel, the Festival was officially opened.

In attendance were Mr. Vu Dai Thang, Member of the Party Central Committee, Deputy Secretary of the Hanoi Party Committee, and Chairman of the Hanoi People's Committee; Mr. Vo Van Hung, Deputy Minister of Agriculture and Environment; Mr. Bui Duy Cuong, Vice Chairman of the Hanoi People's Committee; and Mr. Sundeep Kumar, WCC Vice President for Asia and Co-chair of the World Craft Cities subcommittee, alongside WCC representatives, ambassadors, international organizations, experts, and craft associations.
The presence of leaders from the central government and the capital side-by-side with the world's craft community underlined the political commitment behind Vietnam's craft villages.
In his opening speech, Mr. Cuong described craft villages as a source of jobs, livelihoods, and Thang Long-Hanoi's cultural identity.
Conservation, he stressed, means more than keeping products: it means safeguarding knowledge, skills, and cultural spaces, and making sure young people can carry them forward.

He set out the city's priority of developing craft villages together with the green and circular economies, tourism, and cultural industries, and called for better design, higher quality, and stronger environmental protection without losing local identity.
He also expressed a hope for practical international cooperation in training, design, and technology, to help Vietnamese products reach export markets.
The World Craft Council responded with a strong vote of confidence.
Mr. Kumar called Hanoi a key strategic partner of the Council and proposed signing an MoU with the city.

He put forward two initiatives that would place Hanoi at the center of the global craft network: a World Craft Center in Hanoi, connecting artisans, designers, researchers, and businesses internationally, and a World Craft Academy, bringing master artisans into universities and design schools as teachers.

After the opening ceremony, leaders toured the exhibition, watching young potters at the wheel, meeting artisans, and exploring Van Phuc silk - a direct show of support for the people who keep these crafts alive.

The Festival reflected a clear direction from the central government to the capital: craft villages are to be preserved as part of the nation's cultural identity and, at the same time, developed into a modern economic sector.
For Vietnam, this means linking craft villages with the green and circular economies, sustainable rural livelihoods, tourism, and cultural industries.

For Hanoi, which aims to grow the production value of its craft villages by around 10 per cent a year in 2025-2030, it means building brands, training a new generation of artisans, and strengthening the competitiveness of Hanoi products on world markets.

The first Global Craft Village Conservation and Development Festival 2026 is both a celebration and a commitment, honoring master artisans and skilled workers who have kept Vietnam's crafts alive for centuries.
